title: 124. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Converting Temperature Between Celsius and Fahrenheit
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(0^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: Use the formula \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). Substitute \(C=0\): \(F=\frac{9}{5}(0)+32=32\). Therefore, \(0^\circ\text{C}=32^\circ\text{F}\). The alternative omits the Fahrenheit offset of \(32\).
questions.hint: Decide whether the conversion starts on the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(100^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(100^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: Use \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). Substitute \(C=100\): \(F=\frac{9}{5}(100)+32=180+32=212\). Therefore, \(100^\circ\text{C}=212^\circ\text{F}\). Option B omits the addition of \(32\).
questions.hint: Remember that the two scales differ by both an offset and a scale factor.

questions.learningObjective: Convert a temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(50^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius.
questions.explanation: Use \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\). Substitute \(F=50\): \(C=\frac{5}{9}(50-32)=\frac{5}{9}(18)=10\). Therefore, \(50^\circ\text{F}=10^\circ\text{C}\). Option A stops after subtracting \(32\) and does not multiply by \(\frac{5}{9}\).
questions.hint: Apply the offset and scale factor in the correct order.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(68^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(68^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius.
questions.explanation: Use \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\). Substitute \(F=68\): \(C=\frac{5}{9}(68-32)=\frac{5}{9}(36)=20\). Therefore, \(68^\circ\text{F}=20^\circ\text{C}\). Option A is the result of subtracting \(32\) only.
questions.hint: Decide whether the conversion starts on the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(25^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: Use \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). Substitute \(C=25\): \(F=\frac{9}{5}(25)+32=45+32=77\). Therefore, \(25^\circ\text{C}=77^\circ\text{F}\). Option A omits the addition of \(32\).
questions.hint: Remember that the two scales differ by both an offset and a scale factor.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(20^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(20^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius, rounded to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Use \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\). Substitute \(F=20\): \(C=\frac{5}{9}(20-32)=\frac{5}{9}(-12)=-\frac{60}{9}\approx-6.67\) (rounded to two decimal places). Therefore, \(20^\circ\text{F}\approx -6.67^\circ\text{C}\). Option B incorrectly stops after subtracting \(32\).
questions.hint: Apply the offset and scale factor in the correct order.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(30^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit using the standard formula.
questions.question: A temperature is \(30^\circ\text{C}\). What is this temperature in Fahrenheit?
questions.explanation: Use \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). Substitute \(C=30\): \(F=\frac{9}{5}(30)+32=54+32=86\). Therefore, \(30^\circ\text{C}=86^\circ\text{F}\). Option B omits the addition of \(32\).
questions.hint: Decide whether the conversion starts on the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(104^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(104^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius.
questions.explanation: Use \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\). Substitute \(F=104\): \(C=\frac{5}{9}(104-32)=\frac{5}{9}(72)=40\). Therefore, \(104^\circ\text{F}=40^\circ\text{C}\). Option B is the result of subtracting \(32\) only.
questions.hint: Remember that the two scales differ by both an offset and a scale factor.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(14^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(14^\circ\text{F}\) to Celsius.
questions.explanation: Use \(C=\frac{5}{9}(F-32)\). Substitute \(F=14\): \(C=\frac{5}{9}(14-32)=\frac{5}{9}(-18)=-10\). Therefore, \(14^\circ\text{F}=-10^\circ\text{C}\). Option A stops after subtracting \(32\) and does not multiply by \(\frac{5}{9}\).
questions.hint: Apply the offset and scale factor in the correct order.

questions.learningObjective: Convert \(-40^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit using the standard formula.
questions.question: Convert \(-40^\circ\text{C}\) to Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: Use \(F=\frac{9}{5}C+32\). Substitute \(C=-40\): \(F=\frac{9}{5}(-40)+32=-72+32=-40\). Therefore, \(-40^\circ\text{C}=-40^\circ\text{F}\). Option B has the wrong sign.
questions.hint: Decide whether the conversion starts on the Celsius or Fahrenheit scale.
